summary: Defines a new mobility option for Proxy Mobile IPv6 that lets the local mobility anchor and the mobile access gateway negotiate Quality-of-Service parameters for a mobile node's traffic. The agreed parameters can be used to police and mark packets and to map to rules in the access network.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like agreeing on which lane of the road a certain delivery truck should use and how fast it may go. Two network helpers talk about it first so the traffic is treated fairly.

questions: what is the pmipv6 qos option
what is a qos service request in proxy mobile ipv6
how do lma and mag negotiate qos
subtitle: How two gateways in a Proxy Mobile IPv6 network agree on the quality of service a mobile device's traffic gets.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 had no way for the local mobility anchor and the mobile access gateway to agree on QoS for a mobile node's traffic, especially when the node moves between cellular and WLAN access.
tldr.mechanism: A new mobility option, the Quality-of-Service option, carries a DSCP value plus optional TLV attributes (bit-rate limits, guaranteed rates, priority, traffic selectors) in existing PMIPv6 signaling, and either side can propose, counter-propose, modify or remove a QoS Service Request.
tldr.outcome: The agreed parameters let both gateways mark and police traffic, and let the access gateway map them to access-technology rules. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 7222 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why PMIPv6 Needs a QoS Option
sections.content:
Mobile operators use Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6, RFC 5213) to manage mobility in the network, so the mobile node itself does not take part. Cellular standards already support QoS differentiation, but policy control and in-band QoS for non-cellular access, such as Wireless LAN, were not covered by the standards of the time. QoS policy handover across access technologies had also received little attention.

The RFC names three operations it supports: keeping QoS classification when a node hands over between cellular and WLAN access, mapping QoS classes between access systems, and setting up QoS policies for new flows started on WLAN. QoS policies travel in-band with PMIPv6 signaling and are enforced on the local mobility anchor (LMA) for downlink traffic and on the mobile access gateway (MAG) and its access network for uplink traffic.

The attributes are not tied to one access technology but are meant to be compatible with 3GPP and IEEE 802.11 WLAN QoS. Further attributes, such as latency or jitter bounds, and the handling of QoS between the MAG and the access network are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones can switch between mobile networks and Wi-Fi. This RFC lets the network keep giving your video call the same priority when you switch.

sections.title: How QoS Is Negotiated
sections.content:
The design builds on the Differentiated Services architecture (RFC 2474 and RFC 2475). The access and home networks are assumed to be DiffServ-enabled, with every node on the path supporting the per-hop behavior for the packet markings. The LMA and the MAG are the tunnel entry and exit points, so they are the natural enforcement points for marking, metering, policing and rate-shaping.

The signaling is strictly between the two mobility entities and creates no per-flow state or signaling to any other node. What gets enabled depends on the subscriber profile and the available network resources. The RFC calls one set of parameters a QoS Service Request, and the QoS option represents exactly one such request.

Two usage patterns are shown. In the LMA-initiated case, the LMA sends an Update Notification (UPN) with a QoS option, the MAG may answer with an Update Notification Acknowledgement (UPA) carrying a revised option, and the LMA can accept the revision with a new UPN. In the MAG-initiated case, the MAG puts the option in a Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and the LMA agrees in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA). Once negotiated, both sides install the QoS rules and the MAG installs them on the access network by access-specific means.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper says, 'I would like this parcel to travel fast.' The other says yes, or 'I can only do a bit slower,' and they settle on a deal both can keep.

sections.title: The QoS Option Format
sections.content:
The Quality-of-Service option is a mobility header option with Type 58. It may appear in PBU, PBA, UPN and UPA messages, and a message may carry several instances, each a separate QoS Service Request. The alignment requirement is 4n.

Its fixed fields are Type, Length, an 8-bit SR-ID (Service Request Identifier), a TC (Traffic Class) field, an 8-bit OC (Operational Code) and reserved bits, followed by zero or more QoS attributes. The SR-ID is unique within a mobility session and is always allocated by the LMA. A MAG starting a new request sends 0 and the LMA returns the allocated value.

The Traffic Class field holds a 6-bit DSCP and 2 reserved bits. Without a Traffic Selector attribute the DSCP applies to every flow of the mobility session. The Operational Code says what is being asked: RESPONSE (0), ALLOCATE (1), DE-ALLOCATE (2), MODIFY (3), QUERY (4) or NEGOTIATE (5, a counter proposal). Values 6 to 255 are unused and the receiver MUST ignore an option carrying them. Reserved bits MUST be set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a short form to fill in: a request number, a priority label, and a box saying whether you are asking, changing, cancelling or answering.

sections.title: QoS Attributes
sections.content:
Each attribute is a TLV with an 8-bit Type and an 8-bit Length. Eleven types are defined, 1 to 11. Most carry a 32-bit unsigned bit rate in bits per second, and each may appear at most once per option except the vendor-specific one.

  • Aggregate maximum bit rates (AMBR): Per-MN (types 1 and 2) apply across all mobility sessions of a mobile node; Per-Session (types 3 and 4) apply to one mobility session; Aggregate-Max (types 6 and 7) apply to all flows of the session or, with a traffic selector, to selected flows.
  • Guaranteed bit rates: Guaranteed-DL and Guaranteed-UL (types 8 and 9) give assured bandwidth for a set of flows.
  • Allocation-Retention-Priority (type 5): a 4-bit Priority Level where 1 is the highest, plus Preemption-Capability and Preemption-Vulnerability bits, used in congestion.
  • QoS-Traffic-Selector (type 10): picks the flows the other attributes apply to, using the binary traffic selector formats of RFC 6088.
  • QoS-Vendor-Specific-Attribute (type 11): carries vendor data, identified by the vendor's enterprise number.

The Per-Session attributes have two flags. The Service (S) flag extends the aggregate to the node's other sessions sharing the same Service Identifier, for example a 3GPP Access Point Name, and MUST NOT be 1 when the session has no Service Identifier. The Exclude (E) flag leaves out flows that have a guaranteed rate. When a Traffic Selector is present, the per-MN and per-session AMBR attributes ignore it.
sections.plainLanguage: The attributes are the rules on the form: a speed limit for everything you use, a reserved fast lane for the important call, and a pass saying who goes first when the road is jammed.

sections.title: How the LMA and MAG Behave
sections.content:
Both gateways keep the negotiated requests in their existing tables (the Binding Cache on the LMA, the Binding Update List on the MAG). Each entry holds the SR-ID, the DSCP and the attributes.

When a request arrives with ALLOCATE, the receiver decides using its policy and available resources. If it can meet all requests it acknowledges with status 0, copies the option content back with the code set to RESPONSE, and should enforce the rules on uplink and downlink traffic. If it cannot meet any, it answers with the status CANNOT_MEET_QOS_SERVICE_REQUEST and no QoS options. If it can only offer less, it returns the options it can support with updated values and the code NEGOTIATE, and the requester may agree by resending its message. Conflicting attributes, such as a per-session uplink maximum lower than the guaranteed uplink rate, count as unsupported.

A denial MUST NOT remove the mobility session. Either side can later send MODIFY, DE-ALLOCATE or QUERY. For a query the option carries no attributes, with SR-ID 0 and DSCP 0. Removing a session releases its QoS resources. On an inter-MAG handover (HI hint 3), the LMA includes the active QoS options in the PBA so the new MAG can allocate resources on the new path.
sections.plainLanguage: If the answer is 'yes', they shake on it. If it is 'not that much', they offer a smaller deal. Saying no to the deal never kicks you off the network.

sections.title: Cellular and WLAN Inter-Working
sections.content:
Section 6 describes the target use: carrying the QoS information that 3GPP uses so that it can be enforced when a node is attached to WLAN or has moved from 3GPP to WLAN. The QoS option MUST at least carry a DSCP, which should correspond to the 3GPP QoS Class Index (QCI). The RFC gives example parameter sets for a default non-GBR bearer, a dedicated GBR bearer (QCI 1 to 4, DSCP EF or AF41, with guaranteed and maximum rates) and a dedicated non-GBR bearer (QCI 5 to 9).

A policy control function may supply the policies, or static defaults may be configured on the LMA. When a flow-level rule exists, it overrules the aggregate per-node or per-session rules, as long as the AMBR limits are met. Where the WLAN controller is separate from the MAG, the two need a protocol for QoS inter-working, which the RFC leaves out of scope. The appendices give 3GPP mapping tables, IEEE 802.11e notes and a broadband network gateway scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: When your phone hops from the mobile network to Wi-Fi, the new network is told what priority your call had so it can keep the same deal.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The option travels in PBU, PBA, UPN and UPA messages like any other mobility header option. The RFC states that the security considerations of RFC 5213 and RFC 7077 apply to those messages, and that the option does not require additional security considerations.

IANA allocated mobility option type 58, created a new Quality-of-Service Attribute registry, and assigned values for the new codes. CANNOT_MEET_QOS_SERVICE_REQUEST is 179 for the Proxy Binding Acknowledgement and 130 for the Update Notification Acknowledgement, and the Update Notification reason QOS_SERVICE_REQUEST is 5. Attribute values 12 to 254 are unassigned, to be allocated under the Specification Required policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The request rides in the same sealed envelopes the gateways already use, so it needs no extra lock.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length in octets, excluding Type and Length.

fields.name: SR-ID
fields.desc: Service Request Identifier, allocated by the LMA.

fields.name: OC
fields.desc: Operational Code: the kind of QoS request.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Sent as 0, ignored by the receiver.
